request.system:
You explain a fitted credit-risk model to a credit risk manager who is not a data scientist. You receive the facts about one model and write a short explanation of what drives its predictions of default.

# The text

- Write 5 to 8 sentences in plain English, most important drivers first.
- Mention an interaction when it matters for the model's predictions.
- Say only what the facts support. Do not round a weak effect up to a strong one, and do not add knowledge about credit risk that the facts do not show.
- When the facts do not settle something, say so ("the data do not settle whether ...") or leave it out.

# The answer

Return one JSON object with one list, `sentences`, each with an `id` (1, 2, 3, ...) and its `text`.
messages:
These are the facts about the model.

Model: a gradient-boosted tree model of depth 2 (XGB2), fitted to predict whether a credit applicant defaults (30,000 applicants). Effects are on the log-odds scale: positive values raise the risk of default. Every band is a 95% band from 100 refits of the model on resampled data.

Features, in the order of their share of the model's importance:
- `PAY_0`: repayment status in September 2005, the latest month (-1 paid in full, 1 to 9 months of payment delay; -2 and 0 are not in the data dictionary, commonly read as no consumption and revolving credit used).
  Share of importance 26.5% (95% band 24.1% to 35.0%); rank 1 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= -1: -0.1; 0: -0.5; 1: +0.6; >= 2: +2 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +2.35, 95% band [+2.06, +2.49]).
- `LIMIT_BAL`: amount of the given credit in NT dollars, individual and family (supplementary) credit.
  Share of importance 15.4% (95% band 13.9% to 19.9%); rank 2 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 79999: +0.5; 80000-209999: -0.04; 210000-539999: -0.4; >= 540000: -1 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -1.20, 95% band [-1.38, -0.89]).
- `BILL_AMT1`: amount of the bill statement in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 8.0% (95% band 3.8% to 9.9%); rank 3 to 5 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 21288: -0.13; >= 21289: +0.1 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.67, 95% band [+0.30, +0.92]).
- `PAY_AMT1`: amount paid in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 6.1% (95% band 4.6% to 8.7%); rank 3 to 4 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 1736: +0.11247; 1737-10999: -0.14; >= 11000: -0.3 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.47, 95% band [-0.63, -0.22]).
- `AGE`: age in years.
  Share of importance 2.8% (95% band 1.8% to 4.1%); rank 5 to 7 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 50: -0.01; >= 51: +0.2 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.26, 95% band [+0.03, +0.39]).
- `BILL_AMT2`: amount of the bill statement in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 2.6% (95% band 0.4% to 4.9%); rank 5 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.12, 95% band [-0.40, +0.25]).
- `PAY_AMT2`: amount paid in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 2.2% (95% band 0.7% to 4.8%); rank 4 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.09, 95% band [-0.30, +0.03]).
- `PAY_AMT3`: amount paid in July 2005, two months before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 1.1% (95% band 0.4% to 2.5%); rank 6 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.09, 95% band [-0.10, +0.26]).
- `EDUCATION`: education (1 graduate school, 2 university, 3 high school, 4 others; 0, 5 and 6 are not in the data dictionary).
  Share of importance 1.0% (95% band 0.4% to 2.4%); rank 6 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.01, 95% band [-0.09, +0.15]).

Interactions: the model has 36 pairs. The larger ones:
- `PAY_0 & EDUCATION`: share of importance 14.7% (95% band 10.5% to 15.6%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +1.51 (95% band +1.39 to +1.71) when `EDUCATION` = 1, +5.37 (95% band +4.00 to +6.01) when `EDUCATION` = 3.
  Effect of `EDUCATION` from 1 to 3: -0.52 (95% band -0.73 to -0.31) when `PAY_0` = -2, +3.34 (95% band +2.08 to +3.80) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `BILL_AMT1 & AGE`: share of importance 3.5% (95% band 1.3% to 4.4%).
  Effect of `BILL_AMT1` from 0 to 201,000: +1.26 (95% band +0.41 to +1.51) when `AGE` = 23, +0.23 (95% band -0.10 to +0.59) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.80 (95% band +0.21 to +0.92) when `BILL_AMT1` = 0, -0.23 (95% band -0.53 to +0.19) when `BILL_AMT1` = 201,000.
- `PAY_0 & AGE`: share of importance 1.5% (95% band 0.1% to 2.3%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.32 (95% band +2.06 to +2.56) when `AGE` = 23, +2.24 (95% band +1.94 to +2.40) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.35 (95% band +0.05 to +0.54) when `PAY_0` = -2, +0.28 (95% band +0.01 to +0.38) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `PAY_0 & PAY_AMT1`: share of importance 1.0% (95% band 0.3% to 1.5%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.17 (95% band +1.88 to +2.36) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, +2.71 (95% band +2.14 to +2.71) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.79 (95% band -0.81 to -0.25) when `PAY_0` = -2, -0.25 (95% band -0.47 to -0.03) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `LIMIT_BAL & AGE`: share of importance 1.0% (95% band 0.4% to 1.9%).
  Effect of `LIMIT_BAL` from 20,000 to 430,000: -1.19 (95% band -1.32 to -0.65) when `AGE` = 23, -1.28 (95% band -1.57 to -0.90) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.37 (95% band +0.14 to +0.53) when `LIMIT_BAL` = 20,000, +0.28 (95% band -0.26 to +0.48) when `LIMIT_BAL` = 430,000.
- `PAY_AMT2 & PAY_AMT3`: share of importance 0.9% (95% band 0.0% to 1.0%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT2` from 0 to 19,000: +0.02 (95% band -0.22 to +0.21) when `PAY_AMT3` = 0, -0.13 (95% band -0.38 to +0.03) when `PAY_AMT3` = 17,600.
  Effect of `PAY_AMT3` from 0 to 17,600: +0.13 (95% band -0.11 to +0.30) when `PAY_AMT2` = 0, -0.03 (95% band -0.28 to +0.23) when `PAY_AMT2` = 19,000.
- `PAY_0 & LIMIT_BAL`: share of importance 0.9% (95% band 0.7% to 2.1%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.27 (95% band +1.93 to +2.53) when `LIMIT_BAL` = 20,000, +2.37 (95% band +2.03 to +2.59) when `LIMIT_BAL` = 430,000.
  Effect of `LIMIT_BAL` from 20,000 to 430,000: -1.17 (95% band -1.36 to -0.84) when `PAY_0` = -2, -1.07 (95% band -1.36 to -0.63) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `PAY_AMT1 & EDUCATION`: share of importance 0.9% (95% band 0.1% to 1.8%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.43 (95% band -0.59 to -0.21) when `EDUCATION` = 1, -0.72 (95% band -0.89 to -0.25) when `EDUCATION` = 3.
  Effect of `EDUCATION` from 1 to 3: +0.18 (95% band -0.00 to +0.37) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, -0.11 (95% band -0.17 to +0.14) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.
- `AGE & BILL_AMT2`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 2.0%).
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.14 (95% band +0.03 to +0.42) when `BILL_AMT2` = 0, +0.10 (95% band -0.24 to +0.37) when `BILL_AMT2` = 195,000.
  Effect of `BILL_AMT2` from 0 to 195,000: +0.14 (95% band -0.29 to +0.36) when `AGE` = 23, +0.09 (95% band -0.51 to +0.20) when `AGE` = 53.
- `PAY_AMT1 & PAY_AMT3`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 0.8%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.51 (95% band -0.63 to -0.23) when `PAY_AMT3` = 0, -0.36 (95% band -0.64 to -0.17) when `PAY_AMT3` = 17,600.
  Effect of `PAY_AMT3` from 0 to 17,600: -0.04 (95% band -0.12 to +0.29) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, +0.11 (95% band -0.18 to +0.32) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.
- `PAY_0 & PAY_AMT3`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 1.6%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.25 (95% band +1.97 to +2.46) when `PAY_AMT3` = 0, +2.60 (95% band +2.08 to +2.73) when `PAY_AMT3` = 17,600.
  Effect of `PAY_AMT3` from 0 to 17,600: -0.11 (95% band -0.32 to +0.22) when `PAY_0` = -2, +0.24 (95% band -0.05 to +0.30) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `LIMIT_BAL & BILL_AMT1`: share of importance 0.7% (95% band 0.2% to 1.1%).
  Effect of `LIMIT_BAL` from 20,000 to 430,000: -1.24 (95% band -1.44 to -0.79) when `BILL_AMT1` = 0, -1.51 (95% band -1.79 to -0.65) when `BILL_AMT1` = 201,000.

content.text: {"sentences":[{"id":1,"text":"The model's predictions of default are driven mainly by the applicant's repayment status in the latest month (PAY_0), which accounts for about 26.5% of the model's importance; being two or more months behind on payments adds roughly +2 to the log-odds of default, while paying in full lowers it slightly."},{"id":2,"text":"The size of the applicant's credit limit (LIMIT_BAL) is the second most important driver, about 15.4% of importance: higher limits are associated with lower predicted default risk, with the effect falling by roughly 1.2 log-odds from the 5th to the 95th percentile of limits."},{"id":3,"text":"The effect of repayment status depends strongly on education: the jump in risk from PAY_0 = -2 to 2 is about +1.5 log-odds for graduate-school applicants but about +5.4 for high-school applicants, so these two features should be read together rather than separately."},{"id":4,"text":"Bill amount in the latest month (BILL_AMT1), payment amount in the latest month (PAY_AMT1), and age each contribute smaller effects, with higher bills and older age nudging risk up and larger payments nudging it down."},{"id":5,"text":"The bill-amount effect also interacts with age: a higher latest bill raises predicted risk noticeably for younger applicants (age 23) but only slightly for older ones (age 53), while the age effect is uncertain in size."},{"id":6,"text":"The remaining features, including earlier bill and payment amounts and education on its own, show effects the data do not resolve reliably at this sample size, so they should not be treated as meaningful drivers."},{"id":7,"text":"Many of the interaction terms are small, and several of their uncertainty bands are wide, so the data do not settle the exact size of the weaker interactions."}]}
